title: Jeremiah 18:1–17
context: The LORD sends Jeremiah to the potter’s house, where a marred vessel is reshaped as the potter sees fit. The LORD then speaks to the house of Israel: as clay in the potter’s hand, so are they in his. He declares that if a nation he has threatened turns from evil, he will relent, and if a nation he has promised to bless does evil, he will relent of the good. Jeremiah is sent to call Judah to return, but the people answer that it is in vain and that they will follow their own plans. The LORD then laments that his people have forgotten him and announces scattering. Both traditions read the potter image as a declaration of God’s authority and of the seriousness of his call to repent. Romans 9:21 later uses the potter image, and the existing boxes at Romans 9:21, 1 Samuel 15:29, Jonah 3:10, and Judges 10:16 already treat how the traditions read the potter and God’s relenting.

verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying, Arminian readers note that the passage begins with the LORD initiating the message, so what follows carries his authority, not Jeremiah’s own invention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the formula introduces a new prophetic unit. The word comes to Jeremiah, and the narrative will show how God teaches through an ordinary scene in a craftsman’s workshop.

verses.text: “Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words. Arminian readers see the LORD using a visual lesson, meeting Jeremiah and the people through what they can see.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD chooses the place where his word will be heard. The potter’s house becomes a classroom in which God’s relationship to his people is displayed.

verses.text: Then I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making something on the wheels.
verses.arminianNotes: he was making something on the wheels. Arminian readers see Jeremiah’s prompt obedience, a prophet who goes where he is sent before he understands why.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Jeremiah reports the scene in the first person. The ordinary sight of a potter at work becomes the setting for a profound word about God’s authority.

verses.text: When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
verses.arminianNotes: When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, Arminian readers see hope in the image: a marred vessel is not discarded but reshaped.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase as seemed good to the potter to make it, stressing the potter’s freedom. The image prepares for the LORD’s declaration about his authority over Israel.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Then the LORD’s word came to me, saying, Arminian readers stress that the lesson is not left to Jeremiah’s own interpretation; the LORD himself explains what the potter’s work means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the visual scene is followed by an interpreting word. In prophetic signs, God’s spoken word gives the meaning of what is seen.

verses.text: “House of Israel, can’t I do with you as this potter?” says the LORD. “Behold, as the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: House of Israel, can’t I do with you as this potter? Arminian readers read the potter in light of the conditions that follow in 18:7-10, as the Romans 9:21 box notes, seeing God’s authority exercised in response to a nation’s turning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereign right over his people, as clay in the potter’s hand. The Romans 9:21 box records how Paul’s later use of the potter is read in both traditions.

verses.text: At the instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy it,
verses.arminianNotes: At the instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy it, Arminian readers see a real announcement of judgment that remains open to the nation’s response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the pairing recalls Jeremiah’s commission in 1:10, though the English wording there differs. They read the announcement as genuine, while holding that God’s responses unfold within his eternal purpose.

verses.text: if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them.
verses.arminianNotes: If that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. Arminian readers see God genuinely responding to free repentance, as discussed in the Jonah 3:10 box.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read repent here as describing God’s turning from announced judgment in human terms, without change in his nature or plan. The 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10 boxes set out both readings.

verses.text: At the instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it,
verses.arminianNotes: to build and to plant it, Arminian readers see promises of blessing as real offers, given within a covenant relationship that calls for continued faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language of building and planting also comes from Jeremiah’s commission (1:10). The promise is sincere, and God’s purposes stand behind both his warnings and his blessings.

verses.text: if they do that which is evil in my sight, that they don’t obey my voice, then I will repent of the good with which I said I would benefit them.
verses.arminianNotes: If they do that which is evil in my sight, that they don’t obey my voice, then I will repent of the good with which I said I would benefit them. Arminian readers stress that blessing can be forfeited through persistent disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning as a real means God uses to call his people to obedience. The Judges 10:16 box also treats how God’s responsiveness relates to his unchanging character.

verses.text: “Now therefore, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, ‘The LORD says: “Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a plan against you. Everyone return from his evil way now, and amend your ways and your doings.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Now therefore, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Arminian readers see the conditional principle applied at once: the LORD announces disaster yet pleads, return from his evil way now.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the call to amend your ways and your doings is sincere and urgent. Both traditions hear in it God’s genuine invitation alongside his warning.

verses.text: But they say, ‘It is in vain; for we will walk after our own plans, and we will each follow the stubbornness of his evil heart.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: But they say, ‘It is in vain; for we will walk after our own plans, Arminian readers see a deliberate refusal: the people reject the offered mercy and choose the stubbornness of their own hearts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the stubbornness of his evil heart as the root problem the prophets expose. The Deuteronomy 5:29 box treats how the traditions read God’s longing for obedience and the people’s refusal.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says: “Ask now among the nations, ‘Who has heard such things?’ The virgin of Israel has done a very horrible thing.
verses.arminianNotes: Ask now among the nations, ‘Who has heard such things?’ Arminian readers hear the LORD’s astonishment that his own people have done what even the nations would not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the virgin of Israel, a title of covenant intimacy, has done a very horrible thing. The image heightens the betrayal of a people who belonged to God.

verses.text: Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Will the cold waters that flow down from afar be dried up?
verses.arminianNotes: Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Arminian readers see the reliability of nature set against the unreliability of Israel’s loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse is difficult in detail, but its point seems clear: creation keeps its course while God’s people abandon theirs. Interpreters render the second line in different ways.

verses.text: For my people have forgotten me. They have burned incense to false gods. They have been made to stumble in their ways in the ancient paths, to walk in byways, in a way not built up,
verses.arminianNotes: For my people have forgotten me. They have burned incense to false gods. Arminian readers see forgetting as a moral choice, a turning from the ancient paths to byways of their own making.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of the ancient paths, which resembles the call to ask for the old paths in 6:16. Leaving them for unbuilt roads pictures idolatry as both sin and folly.

verses.text: to make their land an astonishment, and a perpetual hissing. Everyone who passes by it will be astonished, and shake his head.
verses.arminianNotes: To make their land an astonishment, and a perpetual hissing. Arminian readers see judgment as the bitter fruit of the people’s chosen path, a land that others pass by in shock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that astonishment and hissing recur in Jeremiah (19:8). The shaking of heads by passersby marks a public disgrace before the watching nations.

verses.text: I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy. I will show them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.
verses.arminianNotes: I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy. Arminian readers see the scattering as the consequence of refusal, the reverse of the planting God had offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the solemn phrase I will show them the back, and not the face. Withdrawal of God’s face is the opposite of the priestly blessing, a sign of covenant judgment.
